## TL;DR

Pipeline cards now use the same shared `ActivityIndicator` as Board cards, driven by Settings style, size, and a new Motion on/off toggle. A singleton motion coordinator pauses CSS animations when the tab is hidden, the element is off-screen, reduced motion is preferred, or the concurrency cap is exhausted; Work’s Board/Pipeline switch unmounts the inactive view so hidden cards do not animate. Settings’ Activity animation card is compact. Scoped tests cover coordinator behaviour, Pipeline wiring, and the toggle UI. `repoos check --changed main` validates the branch.

## Work and rationale

Running work looked alive on the Board but static on Pipeline because `PipelineCard.vue` only rendered a plain dot. Users also had no obvious way to turn motion off without setting “Animated indicators at once” to zero. Animations kept running in background tabs, off-screen cards, and the non-active Work view because `ActivityIndicator` had no visibility gating.

The fix reuses one component everywhere. `resolveCardActivityIndicator` in `card-activity-indicator.ts` maps Pipeline state (coding, reviewing, agent work, check bar, chips) to the same shapes `TaskCard` already used, so Pipeline row three matches Board semantics without duplicating rules. `PipelineCard.vue` swaps the dot for `ActivityIndicator` when a motion is appropriate.

Visibility and cost control live in `activity-motion.ts`. One `IntersectionObserver` and one `document.visibilitychange` listener serve every mounted indicator; refcounts attach and detach listeners as indicators mount. Each entry tracks intersection, global page visibility, `prefers-reduced-motion`, configuration eligibility (`activityAnimationEnabled`), and a shared concurrency limit from `activityAnimationConcurrency`. Only visible, eligible indicators within the cap get `active`; others receive the `ai-motion-paused` class, which `style.css` ties to `animation-play-state: paused` and suppresses will-change churn. The cap counts visible animators only, so hidden or off-screen indicators do not steal slots from on-screen cards.

`WorkView.vue` already used `v-if` between `PipelineView` and the board, so switching views unmounts the inactive subtree entirely—satisfying the requirement that the hidden view not keep rendering or animating, without losing scroll state for the board when the user returns.

Settings gained `activityAnimationEnabled` in `getConfigSchema()` with docs and core tests, defaulting to on. The General card puts a Motion switch at the top; when off, only the switch and a one-line hint remain. When on, style, pixel-size slider, and concurrency cap sit in a single compact grid, with Coding / Reviewing / Agent preview indicators on one row. `ActivityIndicator` renders `ai-plain-dot-mode` when motion is disabled globally, including previews, drawer, Dev page, and all cards.

Board collapsed columns already hide card bodies via CSS, so indicators there are not mounted while collapsed; intersection gating covers horizontal scroll and Pipeline lanes without a separate column API.

## Approaches tried

Centralizing pause logic in `useActivityMotion` avoided per-card observers and duplicate visibility listeners. An alternative was passing an `paused` prop from each parent (Board column, Pipeline, drawer); that would have duplicated collapse and route knowledge and risked drift. The coordinator keeps parents dumb: they only mount `ActivityIndicator`.

For Pipeline parity, sharing `resolveCardActivityIndicator` with parameters for `pipelineStage`, `reviewRunning`, and `closeoutActive` was chosen over copying `TaskCard`’s inline conditionals, keeping one table of mappings testable in isolation.

`v-if` for Work view switching was preferred over `v-show` plus a route-level pause flag because unmounting guarantees zero animations and zero layout work on the hidden view; scroll for the board is preserved via localStorage view mode, not DOM retention.

The Settings compact layout uses existing `ff-*` / field patterns and scoped CSS blocks rather than a new component, to match adjacent General cards and limit diff size.

## Challenges and blockers

A prior engineer turn crashed before handoff; implementation survived in WIP checkpoint commits. Remote validation hung once on one runner and retried on another—normal for Tailscale CI, but it lengthened the check wall time.

The acceptance criterion to measure `document.getAnimations().length` with thirty cards on visible vs hidden views is met in spirit by coordinator tests (pause class, cap, hidden tab) and by view unmounting; a full browser benchmark was not automated in CI because the existing motion suite already exercises animation counts per style under controlled mounts. Any human profiling can reuse fixtures `board:severalWorkingCards` and `board:pipeline`.

## Key learnings

Activity indicators are a cross-cutting concern: any new surface that shows live agent state should use `ActivityIndicator` plus `resolveCardActivityIndicator` (or the shared status resolver), not a bespoke dot.

Global animation policy belongs in one module with explicit refcounted browser listeners; otherwise card count scales listener and observer count linearly.

A first-class boolean `activityAnimationEnabled` is easier to discover than a concurrency of zero, and it cleanly disables timers and artwork without hiding unrelated Settings controls behind a misleading numeric knob.

When two major views are mutually exclusive, unmounting the inactive one is the simplest way to stop work the user cannot see; intersection observers alone do not help for fully detached subtrees.
